result.markdown: --- title: "Take-home Exercise 02" author: "Stefanie Felicia" date: "13 October, 2025" date-modified: "last-modified" execute: eval: true echo: true warning: false freeze: true --- ## Background Urban mobility is vital to urban planners as they describe how goods and people move within and between cities through all kinds of transportation (e.g. walking, vehicle, bicycle, etc). With good urban planning, proper resources to build roads and . can create smart, efficient and sustainable networks. This led to reduced congestion in roads, reduce carbon emission and smooth travel through roads. The emergence of autonomous vehicles and shared mobility services ash further driven the evolution of public transportation systems. Especially as digital urban infrastructures dataset become available in the internet, we can track for movement pattern across space and time. With this, we can get better understanding and make informed decision to allocate resources. ## Objective In this hands-on, we'll be analyzing LMSA (Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation) to identify specific locations within a map that show significant spatial clustering of similar or dissimilar values. Then, we'll look at hotspots (high values clustered together), coldspots (low values clustered together) and outliers (high values surrounded by low values, or the opposite). So we can discover local insights (mobility pattern across neighbourhoods) instead of global summary measures. We'll also be analyzing EHSA (Emerging Hot Spots Analysis) to complement LMSA. We'll use space-time cube to identify and categorize clusters (coldspots or hotspots) **over time**. Through EHSA, we can spot for bus mobility pattern (trend) over time. In this hands-on, we'll be analyzing geographical distribution of passegner trips in the following time period:\ - Weekday morning peak from 6am to 9am - Weekday afternoon peak from 5pm to 8pm - Weekend/holiday from 11am to 8pm ## The Data In this hands on exercise, we'll be using the following dataset: - Passenger Volume by Origin Destination Bus Stops from LTA DataMall - Bus Stop Location from LTA DataMall - Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea) from data.gov.sg ## Load Required Libraries ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pacman::p_load(tidyverse, sf, sfdep, spdep, tmap, knitr, DT, kableExtra, cluster, factoextra, purrr, Kendall) ``` ::: In this exercise, we'll be using the following libraries: - sf: simple features in R to encode and analyze spatial vector data - spdep: create spatial weights matrix object from polygon 'contiguities' - tmap: used to draw thematic map - tidyverse: collection of R packages that for data manipulation and visualization - knitr: dynamic report generation - cluster: methods for cluster analysis - factoextra: provide easy to use function to extract and visualize the output of multivariate data analysis ## Import Data First, we'll import the cleaned Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea) dataset that we saved on Hand-on 2. Data preparation for this data can be found in my Hands-on 2. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mpsz = read_rds("data/rds/mpsz_cl.rds") ``` ::: Next, we'll import the Bus Stop Location using st_read() and transform the data to EPSG 3414 (projected system for Singapore) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} BusStop = st_read(dsn = "data/LTADataMall/", layer = "BusStop") %>% st_transform(crs = 3414) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Reading layer `BusStop' from data source `C:\stefanie-fel\ISSS626-GAA\Take-home_Ex\Take-home_Ex02\data\LTADataMall' using driver `ESRI Shapefile' Simple feature collection with 5172 features and 2 fields Geometry type: POINT Dimension: XY Bounding box: xmin: 3970.122 ymin: 26482.1 xmax: 48285.52 ymax: 52983.82 Projected CRS: SVY21 ``` ::: ::: Lastly, we'll use read_csv() to import the Passenger Volume by Origin Destination Bus Stops data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} odbus <- read_csv("data/origin_destination_bus_202508.csv") ``` ::: ## Data Preparation First, let's visualize the bus stop points in Singapore to get better understanding of the data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tm_shape(mpsz) + tm_polygons(col = "lightgrey", border.col = "white") + tm_shape(BusStop) + tm_dots(ol="red", size = 0.1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Since the visualization includes bus stops that are outside of Singapore, we should combine both geometry data and data points using st_joins. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} BusStop_in_SG <- st_join( BusStop, mpsz, join = st_within, left = FALSE) names(BusStop_in_SG) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "BUS_STOP_N" "LOC_DESC" "REGION_N" "PLN_AREA_N" "SUBZONE_N" [6] "SUBZONE_C" "geometry" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tm_shape(mpsz) + tm_polygons(col = "lightgrey", border.col = "white") + tm_shape(BusStop_in_SG) + tm_dots(ol="red", size = 0.1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: As can be seen, now the bus stops that are not located outside the map is now gone. Next, we'll create grid layer and take hexagon with bus stops and exclude those areas without bus stop ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hexagon <- st_make_grid(mpsz, cellsize = 375, # diameter is 375 from center to edge what = "polygon", # returns hexagon layer square = FALSE) %>% st_sf() # make large sfc_polygon data into sf tabular (list) dataframe ``` ::: Since the hexagon table only have 1 column which is the polygon data, we need to assign id to each hexagon to know which it is. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hexagon$n_collisions = #return true or false if hexagon intersect the bus stop lengths(st_intersects(hexagon, BusStop_in_SG)) hexagon <- filter(hexagon, n_collisions > 0) # filter to only store hexagons that has bus stop ``` ::: ::: callout-note - `hexagon$n_collisions` returns if hexagon intersects the bus stop - `lengths(st_intersects(hexagon, busStop_in_SG))` : st_intersections return output of geomteric cut, while this function return true or false (in numerical value; 0 means none or values \> 1 meaning the total number of bus stops within the hexagon), - `filter(hexagon, n_collisions > 0)` : filter to only store hexagons that has bus stop ::: Next, we'll drop the n-collisions column and create new column in the data frame to identify unique bus stop locations through IDs. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hexagon <- hexagon %>% select(, -n_collisions) hexagon$HEX_ID <- sprintf( "H%04d", seq_len(nrow(hexagon))) %>% # start with 0 as.factor() #ordinal scale kable(head(hexagon)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |geometry |HEX_ID | |:------------------------------|:------| |POLYGON ((3980.038 28051.92... |H0001 | |POLYGON ((4355.038 28701.44... |H0002 | |POLYGON ((4542.538 30325.23... |H0003 | |POLYGON ((4542.538 30974.75... |H0004 | |POLYGON ((4730.038 30000.47... |H0005 | |POLYGON ((4917.538 28376.68... |H0006 | ::: ::: ## Preparing Trip Generation Data ### Cleaning Data Next, we'll derive create a new variable that stores location of the bus stop, hour of the day and total trips through the bus stop. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} trips <- odbus %>% select(c(ORIGIN_PT_CODE, DAY_TYPE, TIME_PER_HOUR, TOTAL_TRIPS)) %>% rename(BUS_STOP_N = ORIGIN_PT_CODE) %>% rename(HOUR_OF_DAY = TIME_PER_HOUR) %>% rename(TRIPS = TOTAL_TRIPS) trips$BUS_STOP_N <- as.factor(trips$BUS_STOP_N) # so that it cannot be converted accidentally to numerical column kable(head(trips)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |BUS_STOP_N |DAY_TYPE | HOUR_OF_DAY| TRIPS| |:----------|:----------------|-----------:|-----:| |84671 |WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY | 9| 3| |10099 |WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY | 13| 31| |64601 |WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY | 21| 3| |53009 |WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY | 16| 10| |80051 |WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY | 18| 4| |70031 |WEEKDAY | 14| 1| ::: ::: Next, we'll combine the bus stop and hexagon layer data and drop the geometry since we'll be hexagon instead ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # combine bus stop and hexagon (layer) data bs_hex <- st_intersection( BusStop, hexagon) %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% #geometry will be replaced with hexagon select(c(BUS_STOP_N, HEX_ID)) kable(head(bs_hex)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | |BUS_STOP_N |HEX_ID | |:----|:----------|:------| |3092 |25059 |H0001 | |2439 |25751 |H0002 | |241 |26379 |H0003 | |2258 |26369 |H0004 | |2650 |25719 |H0005 | |2651 |25711 |H0005 | ::: ::: ### Add HEX_ID into bus trip data We'll also combine the trips variable with the HEX_ID (location) to finish our data preparation step. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} trips <- inner_join(trips, bs_hex) ``` ::: ### Filter Data for Weekday Morning Peak Next, we'll filter for the weekday morning peak data and combine it back with its hexagon geometry since we also want to know where each bus stop is located and not just its ID. Since previously, we also grouped the data to aggregate the number of trips in each bus stop location, we'll ungroup it so that we can perform analysis on the data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} weekday_morning <- trips %>% filter(DAY_TYPE == 'WEEKDAY'& HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(6, 7, 8, 9)) %>% group_by( BUS_STOP_N, HEX_ID, HOUR_OF_DAY) %>% summarise(TRIPS = sum(TRIPS)) weekday_morning <- left_join(weekday_morning, hexagon) weekday_morning_ungroup <- st_as_sf(weekday_morning) %>% ungroup() ``` ::: Next, we'll also plot the trend of trips in each bus stop location per hour (from 6am to 9am). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} weekday_morning_ungroup <- weekday_morning_ungroup %>% mutate(title_hour = paste0("Hour of day: ", HOUR_OF_DAY, ":00")) tm_shape(weekday_morning_ungroup) + tm_polygons(col = "TRIPS", palette = "Blues", border.col = "grey", alpha = 0.6) + tm_facets(by="title_hour", free.coords=FALSE, drop.units = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: As can be seen, the range of bus trips per hour is quite big (from 0 to 120,000), with most bus location having 0 to 20,000 trips. There is one point in the north and east in which as the hour goes by becomes darker in color (80,000 to 10,000 bus trip), indicating that a lot of buses pass by or stop on those location. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} weekday_morning_ungroup <- weekday_morning_ungroup %>% select(-title_hour) # drop title_hour as it was used for visualization only ``` ::: We can also check what time of the day where there are most buses and less waiting time. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} weekday_morning_hour <- trips %>% filter(DAY_TYPE == 'WEEKDAY'& HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(6, 7, 8, 9)) %>% group_by( HOUR_OF_DAY) %>% summarise(TRIPS = sum(TRIPS)) weekday_morning_hour ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 2 HOUR_OF_DAY TRIPS 1 6 5090423 2 7 8231834 3 8 7324169 4 9 4554990 ``` ::: ::: As can be seen, 7am and 8am have the most bus trips out of the 6am to 9am time period. ### Filter Data for Weekday Afternoon Peak Just like before, we'll filter for the weekday afternoon peak data (from 5pm to 8pm) and combine it back with its hexagon geometry and ungroup the data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} weekday_afternoon <- trips %>% filter(DAY_TYPE == 'WEEKDAY'& HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(17, 18, 19,20)) %>% group_by( BUS_STOP_N, HEX_ID, HOUR_OF_DAY) %>% summarise(TRIPS = sum(TRIPS)) weekday_afternoon <- left_join(weekday_afternoon, hexagon) weekday_afternoon_ungroup <- st_as_sf(weekday_afternoon) %>% ungroup() weekday_afternoon_ungroup ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Simple feature collection with 19723 features and 4 fields Geometry type: POLYGON Dimension: XY Bounding box: xmin: 3792.538 ymin: 26428.12 xmax: 47292.54 ymax: 50243.82 Projected CRS: SVY21 / Singapore TM # ℹ 19,713 more rows ``` ::: ::: We'll also visualize the filtered data per hour to understand better the trend of bus trips in each region. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} weekday_afternoon_ungroup <- weekday_afternoon_ungroup %>% mutate(title_hour = paste0("Hour of day: ", HOUR_OF_DAY, ":00")) tm_shape(weekday_afternoon_ungroup) + tm_polygons(col = "TRIPS", palette = "Blues", border.col = "grey", alpha = 0.6) + tm_facets(by="title_hour", free.coords=FALSE, drop.units = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Surprisingly, we observe that there are less bus trips during this time period even though it is considered rush hour. We can also see that the same points (in the east and west) from the weekday morning peak also also have high frequency of buses stopping by this location in the afternoon. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} weekday_afternoon_ungroup <- weekday_afternoon_ungroup %>% select(-title_hour) # drop title_hour as it was used for visualization only ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} weekday_afternoon_hour <- trips %>% filter(DAY_TYPE == 'WEEKDAY'& HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(17, 18, 19,20)) %>% group_by( HOUR_OF_DAY) %>% summarise(TRIPS = sum(TRIPS)) weekday_afternoon_hour ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 2 HOUR_OF_DAY TRIPS 1 17 7149274 2 18 8095040 3 19 5601650 4 20 3848416 ``` ::: ::: As expected, on weekdays most people make trips on nearing peak hours and peak hours (5pm and 6pm), while the number starts to drop drastically on 7pm and 8pm. This also indicate that later hours have longer wait time. ### Filter Data for Weekend/holiday We'll filter for the weekend or holiday data (from 11am to 8pm) and combine it back with its hexagon geometry and ungroup the data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} weekend <- trips %>% filter(DAY_TYPE == 'WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY' & HOUR_OF_DAY >= 11 & HOUR_OF_DAY <= 20) %>% group_by( HEX_ID, HOUR_OF_DAY) %>% summarise(TRIPS = sum(TRIPS)) weekend_ungroup <- left_join(weekend, hexagon) weekend_ungroup <- st_as_sf(weekend_ungroup) %>% ungroup() names(weekend_ungroup) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "HEX_ID" "HOUR_OF_DAY" "TRIPS" "geometry" ``` ::: ::: Next, we'll visualize the data to understand better the trend of bus trips in each hour. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} weekend_ungroup <- weekend_ungroup %>% mutate(title_hour = paste("Hour of day: ", HOUR_OF_DAY, ":00")) tm_shape(weekend_ungroup) + tm_polygons(col = "TRIPS", palette = "Blues", border.col = "grey", alpha = 0.6) + tm_facets(by="title_hour", free.coords=FALSE, drop.units = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} weekend_ungroup <- weekend_ungroup %>% select(-title_hour) ``` ::: There are less frequency of bus trips on holidays and weekend, with most of them having 0 to 10,000 bus trips per hour. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} weekend_time <- trips %>% filter(DAY_TYPE == 'WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY' & HOUR_OF_DAY >= 11 & HOUR_OF_DAY <= 20) %>% group_by(HOUR_OF_DAY) %>% summarise(TRIPS = sum(TRIPS)) weekend_time ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 10 × 2 HOUR_OF_DAY TRIPS 1 11 2147794 2 12 2243641 3 13 2156924 4 14 2019550 5 15 2019245 6 16 2115944 7 17 2293242 8 18 2220894 9 19 1948271 10 20 1679202 ``` ::: ::: As can be seen, there are approxamtely similar number of bus trips on the weekend from 11am to 8pm. ## LMSA Analysis In this section, we'll be performing LMSA analysis to identify specific locations in the map that show similar or dissimilar values. LMSA allows us to examine the relationship of each location with its neighbours, which provide deeper insight than the global trend. In this section we'll be using statistic methods such as: - Local Moran's I: to detect outlier and clusters - Getis-Ord: detect hot spots and cold spots ### LMSA Analysis of Bus Trips on Weekday Morning In this section, we'll be performing LMSA analysis of bus bus trips on weekday morning with Local Moran's I to detect outliers (negative value) and cluster (positive value) and Getis-Ord (to detect cold spots and hot spots #### Local Moran's I To perform Local Moran's I, we first need to compute contiguity spatial weights to define the neighbourhood's relationship with each other. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nb_mday <- sfdep::st_contiguity(weekday_morning_ungroup) wt_mday <- sfdep::st_weights(nb_mday, style = "W", allow_zero = TRUE) wm_mday <- weekday_morning_ungroup %>% dplyr::mutate( nb = I(nb_mday), wt = I(wt_mday), .before = 1 ) names(wm_mday) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "nb" "wt" "BUS_STOP_N" "HEX_ID" "HOUR_OF_DAY" [6] "TRIPS" "geometry" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(wm_mday$nb) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Neighbour list object: Number of regions: 19511 Number of nonzero links: 1042186 7787 7788 7789 7790 8059 8060 8061 8062 8063 8064 8065 8066 8067 8068 8069 8070 8211 8212 8213 8214 with 122 links ``` ::: ::: The report identify 19K regions with one area having 20 neighbours. There are also 20 areas that only have 3 neighbours. Next, we'll be computing local Moran's I using local_moran() which compute li values ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1234) moran_mday <- weekday_morning_ungroup %>% mutate(local_moran = local_moran(TRIPS, nb_mday, wt_mday, nsim = 99), .before = 1) %>% unnest(local_moran) ``` ::: Next, we'll map the Local Moran's I values. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tm_shape(moran_mday) + tm_polygons(fill = "ii", fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals( style = "pretty", n = 5, values = "brewer.RdBu"), fill.legend = tm_legend( title = "Local Morans'I", position = tm_pos_out())) + tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) + tm_title("Loal Morans'I of Weekday Morning (Queen's method)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: callout-note - There is a lot of potential outliers and cluster found across Singapore's bus stop, most of bus stops at the edges of Singapore are have quite similar bus trips. But places that are more in the center of Singapore have more outliers. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tm_shape(moran_mday) + tm_polygons(fill = "p_ii", fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals( breaks = c(-Inf, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, Inf), values = "-brewer.Reds"), fill.legend = tm_legend( title = "p-value", position = tm_pos_out())) + tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) + tm_title("p-values of Loal Moran's I of Weekday Morning (Queen's method)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-30-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: callout-note - As can be seen, places in the east (e.g. Tuas, Pioneer and Boon Lay) have similar values as each other (indicated from the p-value that's less than 0.001) - Edges in the east region also have similar values as their p-values are less than 0.001 - North region where there is a lot of outlier also have p-value \<0.001 - North east region and central area surprisingly have less significant observations. ::: Next, we can also visualize the relationship between bus trips and the average values of its neighbours (using sptial lag) to identify spatial autocorrelation. We'll also be performing standardization on the spatial lag and bus trip column to reveal pattern of high-high, high-low, low-high and low-low value clusters. In this code chunk, we'll use st_lag to calculate spatial lag of neighbours. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} moran_mday <- moran_mday %>% mutate(lag_mday = st_lag( TRIPS, nb_mday, wt_mday), .before = 1) %>% unnest(lag_mday) ``` ::: We'll rescale the bus trip column and spatial lag ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} moran_mday <- moran_mday %>% mutate(trips_scaled = scale(TRIPS), scaled_lag_mday = scale(lag_mday), .before = 1) ``` ::: We'll visualize the result using scatterplot to understand the trend of clusters. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = moran_mday, aes(x = trips_scaled, y = scaled_lag_mday, color = mean)) + geom_point(size = 2) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black") + geom_hline(yintercept=mean(moran_mday$scaled_lag_mday), lty=2) + geom_vline(xintercept=mean(moran_mday$morning_weekday_scaled), lty=2) + scale_color_manual( values = c("High-High" = "red", "Low-Low" = "blue", "Low-High" = "lightblue", "High-Low" = "pink")) + labs(x = "Trips", y = "Spatial Lag of GDPPC", title = "Moran Scatterplot with Weekday Morning Quadrants") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-33-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: There are a lot of areas that are high frequency of bus trips surrounded by areas with high bus trips frequency. While low-low, high-low and low-high clusters are not so common during weekday morning. Next, we'll derive the spatially lagged bus trip and center the spatially lagged variable. We'll also create a new column to determine if the observation is insignificant, low-low cluster, low-high-cluster, high-low and high-high cluster. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} alpha <- 0.05 moran_mday <- moran_mday %>% mutate( weekday_morning_cluster = ifelse( p_ii < 0.05, as.character(mean), "Insignificant"), weekday_morning_cluster = factor( weekday_morning_cluster, levels = c("Insignificant", "Low-Low", "Low-High", "High-Low", "High-High") ) ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wmday_map <- tm_shape(moran_mday) + tm_polygons( fill = "weekday_morning_cluster", fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical( values = c( "grey80", # Insignificant "blue", # Low-Low "lightblue", # Low-High "pink", # High-Low "red" # High-High ) ), fill.legend = tm_legend( title = "Weekday Morning Clusters", position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom")) ) + tm_borders() + tm_title("Local Moran's I Clusters (p < 0.05)") wmday_map ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-35-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: As can be seen, places that are edges of Singapore mostly have low-low clusters. While north east regions have most high-high clusters, followed by east regons. #### Getis-Ord The following steps are used to perform Getis ord: 1. Derive spatial weight matrix 2. Compute Gi\* statistics 3. Mapping Gi\* statistics In this exercise, we'll be using adaptive distance weights to derive spatial weight matrix. K-nearest neighbours will be used to control the number of neighbours. So, before we derive the spatial weight matrix, we'll use the elbow method to determine how many number of clusters would be optimal for the analysis. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} trips_col <- "TRIPS" features <- weekday_morning_ungroup %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(all_of(trips_col)) features <- scale(features) # Elbow method fviz_nbclust(features, kmeans, method = "wss") optimal_k <- 0 km <- kmeans(features, centers = optimal_k, nstart = 25) weekday_morning_ungroup$cluster <- factor(km$cluster) # Plot clusters library(ggplot2) ggplot(weekday_morning_ungroup) + geom_sf(aes(fill = cluster)) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: Note: I set the code to `eval = FALSE` because when I run it it works, except the k_optimal gives me an error, but it generated the graph for the results of the elbow method.
